title: Genesis 14. The Cup of War and Blessing.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 14. The Cup of War and Blessing.
War comes.
The first battle in Scripture.
Four kings against five.
Chedorlaomer, king of Elam and three allies against the kings of Sodom,
Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela.
For twelve years the five served the four.
In the thirteenth year, they rebelled.
In the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer came.
He sweeps through the land like a flood.
Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim.
Zuzim in Ham.
Emim in Shaveh Kiriathaim.
Horites in Mount Seir, as far as El Paran.
He turns back to En Mishpat, Kadesh,
and strikes the Amalekites and the Amorites.
The four kings move across the earth like the judgment that preceded them,
nothing stands.
Then the five kings meet them in the valley of Siddim.
The valley is full of tar pits.
The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee.
Some fall into the pits.
The rest flee to the hills.
The victors take all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah,
all their food, and go.
They take Lot, Abram's brother's son, who was living in Sodom,
and his goods, and depart.
The man who chose the garden of the plain,
who moved his tent toward Sodom,
who saw abundance and did not ask who lived in it,
is now carried off by the same armies that swept through the land.
The Cup that was shared in chapter thirteen has been taken.
The man who chose the water is taken with the city's wealth,
as plunder.
One who escaped comes and tells Abram the Hebrew.
He is living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite,
brother of Eshcol and Aner, allies of Abram.
Abram hears that his kinsman is taken captive.
He does not negotiate.
He does not send a message.
He does not wait.
He leads out three hundred and eighteen trained men,
born in his own house, and pursues them as far as Dan.
By night he divides his forces against them, he and his servants,
and strikes them.
He pursues them to Hobah, north of Damascus.
He brings back all the goods.
He brings back Lot, his brother's son, and his goods.
He brings back the women and the people.
The man who gave away his wife in Egypt from fear now pursues four armies by night from love.
The man who could not protect Sarai from Pharaoh protects Lot from Chedorlaomer.
The Cup that was endangered by Abram's weakness in chapter twelve is now defended by Abram's courage in chapter fourteen.
The vessel is not consistent.
But the Cup holds.
On the way back,
the king of Sodom comes out to meet him in the King's Valley.
Then another king appears.
Melchizedek, king of Salem, brings out bread and wine.
He is a priest of God Most High.
He blesses Abram: Blessed be Abram by God Most High,
Possessor of heaven and earth.
And blessed be God Most High,
who has delivered your enemies into your hand.
Bread and wine.
The Cup of war is answered with the Cup of blessing.
The first time bread and wine appear together in Scripture,
they are in the hands of a priest-king whose name means King of Righteousness,
whose city means Peace.
He does not fight.
He does not take.
He brings bread and wine and speaks a blessing.
In a chapter full of kings, nine kings named, four against five,
war and plunder and pursuit and rescue, one king stands apart.
He does not go to war.
He goes to meet the man who won.
Abram gives him a tithe of everything.
The man who received wealth from Pharaoh gives a tenth to Melchizedek.
The Cup that was filled in Egypt is now poured out in Salem.
What was taken from a king who did not know God is given to a priest who does.
Then the king of Sodom speaks: Give me the people.
Keep the goods for yourself.
Abram answers: I have lifted my hand to the Lord,
God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth.
I will not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours,
lest you say, I made Abram rich.
The Cup that could have been filled with Sodom's wealth is left empty,
by choice.
Abram knows the difference between Melchizedek's blessing and Sodom's goods.
One cup was given by a priest of God Most High.
The other is offered by a king whose city will burn.
The same city whose plain looked like the garden of the Lord.
The same city whose men were wicked, great sinners against the Lord.
The king of Sodom offers Abram the spoil of his own city,
and Abram refuses.
I will take nothing, except what the young men have eaten,
and the portion of the men who went with me.
Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre.
Let them take their portion.
Abram will not let Sodom claim what only God can claim.
The man who let Pharaoh say he was Sarai's brother now refuses to let the king of Sodom say he was Abram's benefactor.
The vessel that fumbled in Egypt has learned something.
Not perfectly, not yet.
But here, in this valley,
with the spoil of four armies behind him and the bread and wine of a priest-king still warm in his memory,
Abram draws a line.
Not a thread.
Not a sandal strap.
The Cup is filled by God,
or it is not filled at all.
Melchizedek is gone.
He appeared without genealogy, without origin, without explanation.
He blessed.
He received.
He disappeared.
The Cup of blessing he carried, bread and wine,
the first of their kind, will not appear again in Genesis.
What they mean has not been spoken.
But they were real.
A priest-king from a city called Peace stood in a valley of war and offered bread and wine to a man who had just rescued his nephew from kings,
and the man gave him a tithe,
and then refused everything the king of Sodom could offer.
The chapter ends with Abram in the King's Valley.
He has won a war.
He has received a blessing.
He has refused a fortune.
He has recovered Lot.
But Lot will return to Sodom.
The nephew who was rescued from captivity will go back to the city whose king could not protect him.
The Cup was defended.
The man it was defended for has not yet chosen to stay where the Cup is safe.
